title: SIU clears officers who fatally shot Erixon Kabera eight times in hallway
subtitle: Police fired as many as 24 bullets after Kabera raised what looked like a handgun - but it was a replica
article: Two Hamilton police officers shot at Erixon Kabera upward of 24 times - eight bullets eventually striking him - because the 43-year-old walked toward the officers in his apartment hallway holding up what looked like a handgun.

One of the officers, grazed by a bullet in the back of his head, even initially believed Kabera had fired first. But the black gun in Kabera's hand turned out to be replica and all of the bullets fired down the 47-metre hallway came from police-issued pistols.

"The officers honestly believed they were looking at an actual gun in the complainant's possession," Special Investigations Unit director Joseph Martino wrote in the report released Friday, in which the officers were cleared of wrongdoing in Kabera's death.
"Though mistaken, their misapprehension was a reasonable one."
Kabera, a father of three who was active in the local Rwandan community, died in hospital early on Nov. 10, 2024 - not long after he was shot in the fifth-floor hallway at 1964 Main St. W.
His death spurred a vigil and calls for justice from loved ones and the Rwandan community.

For months, family have been asking for answers as to why the man they knew as a kind community builder was killed. Their demands for transparency were intensified by early confusion, after the SIU initially reported an exchange of gunfire - a claim later retracted when it was confirmed Kabera's weapon was not real.

The SIU report, more than six months after his death, sheds new light on the chaotic confrontation in which one of the officers was grazed by a bullet and both fell down as they fired their weapons. Kabera was shot in the neck, back, hip, arm, stomach and chest.

One of the officers and civilian witnesses participated in the SIU investigation, while the other officer declined to be interviewed, but handed over her notes. The SIU did not name Kabera in the report.
"The family is disappointed with the findings of the investigation," Kabera's family said in a statement shared by law firm Falconers LLP.
"Erixon was loved by many and is deeply missed by his family, friends, and his community both in Canada and in Rwanda."
The family is reviewing the report and considering legal options, the statement said.
In another statement, Hamilton police noted the SIU report concluded the force used by officers was "reasonable under the circumstances."
"As a service, we recognize the profound impact this incident has had on Erixon's family, the broader community and our members," police said.
"For now, our service remains committed to meeting with Erixon's family and Rwandan community leaders to find a path forward whenever the community is ready."

According to the SIU report, police were called to the building around 4:30 p.m. on Nov. 9 by a fifth-floor resident who reported an unfamiliar man knocking on her door. The witness opened the door, but quickly closed and locked it after seeing what appeared to be a handgun in the man's right hand.
Kabera lived in an apartment at the southern end of the fifth-floor hallway, where he walked in and out of his unit several times, approaching his neighbour's door and trying to turn the handle.
He asked to be let in and said he wanted to "hang," the SIU said. But his neighbour largely ignored him, other than to tell him to go away.
Two officers arrived at the building by about 4:50 p.m.
When they got off the elevator on the fifth floor, they called out to Kabera, who entered his apartment and locked the door.

The witness allowed officers insider her apartment, where she explained to police what had happened and described the "gun" as being similar to the police-issued Glock semi-automatic pistol the officers carried. One of the officers kept the door open to keep an eye on Kabera's door.
Within minutes, the SIU said, Kabera exited his apartment with what appeared to be a handgun in his right hand. It was pointed at the floor.
When the officers stepped into the hallway to confront him, the SIU said, Kabera raised the replica gun and walked toward them.
"He was immediately met with gunfire from the officers," the SIU said.

An unidentified female officer, called "Subject Officer 2" in the report, shot as many as eight rounds while moving backward in the hallway. She lost her footing and fell to the floor as Kabera continued to walk forward with the replica gun in his hands.

The other officer, a man called "Subject Officer 1," fired six to eight shots as he also retreated back in the hallway, the SIU said. He told investigators that he believed Kabera fired first, mistakenly believing Subject Officer 2's gunfire came from Kabera.

Martino called this an "an honest but mistaken belief in the highly charged atmosphere that prevailed." Regardless, the officer was "within his rights in shooting at the complainant the moment he raised his hand in the officers' direction seemingly holding a gun."
Despite the shots from police, the SIU said Kabera "remained unfazed."
The male officer also fell, but managed to move back and replace a magazine of bullets. The female officer, who lost her gun when she fell, tried to use her Taser, with no effect.
That's when the male officer fired again - seven to eight shots - and Kabera collapsed and landed on his back, the SIU said.

At 5 p.m., someone could be heard saying over the police radio "drop the gun" and Subject Officer 1 called: "Shots fired, I'm hit, we have one male down; I need units here, I need EMS, I need fire." He said he was bleeding from the back of the head.
The female officer first checked on her colleague and then approached Kabera to render first-aid until paramedics arrived. The SIU said the officer's head injury was a "graze wound."
Kabera was pronounced dead in hospital at 12:47 a.m.

At the scene, SIU investigators found the hallway was littered with cartridge cases, bullet fragments, police equipment, the black gun later found to be a replica, and blood. Kabera's apartment door was open and bullets were found inside, on the floor and in the wall.
Testing later showed Kabera's DNA was found on the replica gun, according to the SIU.
An autopsy found Kabera's cause of death was from multiple gunshot wounds. Among his wounds were gunshots to his back.
But Martino said this fact doesn't change his finding that the shooting was justified, because of the "volatility" of the events.

"That is to say, it is not surprising the complainant suffered wounds to the back given the movements of the parties at the time, including the distinct possibility that the complainant might have been falling and rotating to the floor as some of the gunfire took place," he wrote.
The force used by the officers was "reasonable" as the replica gun looked real and Kabera "brandished it as a gun."
